questions.prompt: Arrange the **5-layer Internet (TCP/IP) stack** from TOP to BOTTOM:
questions.explain:
**Application → Transport → Network → Link → Physical.**
Mnemonic: *All Trains Need Loud Pilots*. Each layer uses the service of the one below and serves the one above.

questions.prompt: As data moves DOWN the stack at the sender, each layer:
options: Adds its own header in front of what it received from above (encapsulation)
Removes a header from what it received
questions.explain: **Encapsulation — the Russian-doll rule:** message → segment (TCP/UDP header) → datagram (IP header) → frame (link header+trailer). The receiver peels them off in reverse.

questions.prompt: What is the **network-layer** PDU (protocol data unit) called?
questions.explain: Application = **message** · Transport = **segment** · Network = **datagram/packet** · Link = **frame**. Exam answers require the exact term per layer.

questions.prompt: Which addresses live at which layer?
options: Port numbers = transport, IP addresses = network, MAC addresses = link
IP addresses = transport, MAC = network, ports = link
MAC = network, IP = link, ports = transport
Ports = application, IP = link, MAC = physical
questions.explain: **Port (16-bit) → transport** (which process), **IP (32-bit) → network** (which host, end-to-end), **MAC (48-bit) → link** (which interface, this hop only). IP never changes in transit; MAC changes at every hop.

**TCP:** connection setup, reliability (ACK + retransmit), ordering, flow + congestion control — 20-byte header.
**UDP:** connectionless, best-effort, no ordering, **8-byte header** — used by DNS, DHCP, streaming, VoIP.

questions.prompt: The Internet's network layer offers a ______ service model.
options: best-effort (no guarantees on delivery, order, or timing)
questions.explain: IP is **best-effort**: datagrams can be lost, reordered, duplicated. Any reliability must come from the layer above (TCP) — a favourite 1-mark definition question.

questions.prompt: A frame cannot cross a router because:
options: MAC addresses only have meaning on the local LAN; routers strip the frame and re-frame on the next link
Routers operate only at the physical layer
Frames are too large for routers
IP addresses change at every hop
questions.explain: A router is a **network-layer** device: it removes the link header, makes a forwarding decision on the **IP** datagram, then builds a NEW frame for the next link (new src/dst MAC). IP addresses stay constant end-to-end; MACs are per-hop.

questions.source: CH0 Refresher — TCP vs UDP users
questions.explain: **HTTP needs reliability → TCP.** **DNS favours speed for tiny queries → UDP** (falls back to TCP for big answers/zone transfers). DHCP also uses UDP — remember it for Ch4.
